headline: AIM's second day splits into verticals, and future cities is where construction sits
deck: Concurrent tracks on FDI, portfolio investment, SMEs, startups, family offices, future cities and the digital economy divide the audience by what it buys.
excerpt: AIM Congress runs its sector tracks on the middle day, covering foreign direct investment, portfolio investment, small enterprises, startups, family offices, future cities and the digital economy. Two of those seven have direct construction content.
content:
AIM Congress at Dubai World Trade Centre organises its middle day as concurrent vertical tracks, and for a reader whose interest is physical rather than financial, most of them can be skipped.

The tracks cover foreign direct investment, foreign portfolio investment, small and medium enterprises, startups, family offices, future cities and the digital economy. Of those seven, two produce buildings.

Future cities is the obvious one, and it is a category that needs handling carefully. Urban development conferences have a long history of presenting renderings as programmes, and the distance between a masterplan and a construction contract is measured in years and in changes of scope. What is worth listening for is not the vision but the procurement: who is appointed, what package is tendered, and on what delivery model. A masterplan with a named delivery partner and a tendered enabling works package is a project. One with neither is a proposition.

The digital economy track is the less obvious one and currently the more productive. Data centres are the construction consequence of digital economy investment, and the Emirates has been adding capacity steadily. Each facility is a building with heavy electrical and mechanical content, a grid connection and a cooling plant, and the pipeline across the Gulf now runs to well over a hundred projects.

Foreign direct investment as a track is a policy conversation rather than a project one, but its measure matters. According to the World Investment Report 2026 from the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, the United Arab Emirates recorded inflows of AED 177.3bn in 2025 and retained second place worldwide for new greenfield projects for a third consecutive year with 1,562 of them.

Greenfield is the word that connects the financial and the physical. A greenfield project builds something; an acquisition changes an owner. On a count basis the greenfield measure is the best available proxy for how much construction an investment climate generates, though it treats a regional headquarters and a factory as one project each.

The structure of the congress puts the specifics last. Day three carries bilateral and multilateral signings, country-pavilion deal announcements and the AIM Investment Awards, which is where individual projects acquire a name, a sector and occasionally a value. For contractors and equipment suppliers the useful exercise is to ignore the aggregate figures and count only the announcements that name a facility. A memorandum to explore cooperation commits nobody to pour concrete; a joint venture with a site and a capacity figure eventually does.

The congress runs to 9 September, with more than 20,000 participants and over 400 institutions expected.
